claim: Ninein is a centrosome protein that has been implicated in microtubule anchorage and centrosome cohesion.
source: Ninein is a centrosome protein that has been implicated in microtubule anchorage and centrosome cohesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ninein's functions.

claim: Mutations in the human NINEIN gene have been linked to Seckel syndrome and to a rare form of skeletal dysplasia.
source: Mutations in the human NINEIN gene have been linked to Seckel syndrome and to a rare form of skeletal dysplasia.
evidence: This claim references established associations between NINEIN mutations and human diseases.

claim: Ninein knockout mice exhibit advanced endochondral ossification during embryonic development.
source: Here, we describe a ninein knockout mouse with advanced endochondral ossification during embryonic development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations presented in the manuscript, including skeletal staining data.

claim: The absence of ninein delays the formation of the bone marrow cavity in the prenatal tibia.
source: Although the long bones maintain a regular size, the absence of ninein delays the formation of the bone marrow cavity in the prenatal tibia.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray microtomography data showing differences in bone volume in the central tibia.

claim: Intramembranous ossification in the skull is more developed in ninein-deficient mice, leading to premature closure of the interfrontal suture.
source: Likewise, intramembranous ossification in the skull is more developed, leading to a premature closure of the interfrontal suture.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis and skeletal staining showing increased mineralization and reduced suture space.

claim: Ninein is strongly expressed in osteoclasts of control mice.
source: We demonstrate that ninein is strongly expressed in osteoclasts of control mice
evidence: This claim is supported by β-galactosidase staining in Nintm1a mice showing expression in multinucleated cells identified as osteoclasts.

claim: The absence of ninein reduces the fusion of precursor cells into syncytial osteoclasts.
source: and that its absence reduces the fusion of precursor cells into syncytial osteoclasts
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of TRAP-positive cells showing reduced multinucleated osteoclasts in ninein-deficient samples.

claim: The number of osteoblasts remains unaffected by ninein deficiency.
source: whereas the number of osteoblasts remains unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by alkaline phosphatase staining and quantification showing similar osteoblast numbers in control and mutant embryos.

claim: Ninein-deficient osteoclasts have a reduced capacity to resorb bone.
source: As a consequence, ninein-deficient osteoclasts have a reduced capacity to resorb bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro bone resorption assays showing smaller resorption areas in ninein del/del cultures.

claim: The absence of ninein interferes with centrosomal microtubule organization.
source: At the cellular level, the absence of ninein interferes with centrosomal microtubule organization
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing less focused microtubule arrays in ninein-deficient cells.

claim: The absence of ninein reduces centrosome cohesion.
source: reduces centrosome cohesion
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements showing increased distance between mother and daughter centrioles in ninein-deficient cells.

claim: The absence of ninein provokes the loss of centrosome clustering in multinucleated mature osteoclasts.
source: and provokes the loss of centrosome clustering in multinucleated mature osteoclasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification showing that 93% of control osteoclasts display centriole clustering whereas only 11% of ninein del/del osteoclasts show clustering.

claim: Centrosomal ninein is important for osteoclast fusion to enable a functional balance between bone-forming osteoblasts and bone-resorbing osteoclasts during skeletal development.
source: We propose that centrosomal ninein is important for osteoclast fusion, to enable a functional balance between bone-forming osteoblasts and bone-resorbing osteoclasts during skeletal development.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Constitutive ninein-knockout mice were viable, without obvious abnormalities, and capable of reproduction.
source: Constitutive ninein-knockout mice were viable, without obvious abnormalities, and capable of reproduction (Lecland et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When ninein-deficient animals were intercrossed, a significant reduction in the litter size was observed.
source: However, when ninein-deficient animals were intercrossed, a significant reduction in the litter size was observed (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A comparing litter sizes across different genotype crosses.

claim: Following delivery, nearly one third of the newborn pups were severely growth-retarded with signs of dwarfism.
source: Following delivery, nearly one third of the newborn pups were severely growth-retarded with signs of dwarfism, reminiscent of what is occurring in patients carrying ninein mutations (Dauber et al., 2012; Grosch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on observations of newborn pups and comparison to human patients with ninein mutations.

claim: Most growth-retarded pups identified at birth did not survive, and the neonatal lethality was reaching 35% within 48 hr.
source: Most growth-retarded pups identified at birth did not survive, and the neonatal lethality was reaching 35% within 48 hr.
evidence: This claim is based on observations of pup survival following birth.

claim: Spontaneous delivery occurred generally on the nineteenth day post coitum (dpc) in control females.
source: Whereas spontaneous delivery occurred generally on the nineteenth day post coitum (dpc) in control females
evidence: This claim is based on observations of delivery timing in control mice.

claim: Several ninein-deleted females had difficulty to deliver by the 22nd dpc and were then euthanized.
source: several ninein-deleted females had difficulty to deliver by the 22nd dpc and were then euthanized.
evidence: This claim is based on observations of delivery difficulties in ninein-deleted females.

claim: Examination of the litters from ninein-deleted females that failed to deliver revealed that they never contained more than four pups and that these pups were always dead.
source: Examination of the litters revealed that they never contained more than four pups and that these pups were always dead (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on examination of litters from ninein-deleted females, with supporting image in Figure 1B.

claim: The increased mortality in utero was exclusively dependent on the zygotic genotype.
source: This increased mortality in utero was exclusively dependent on the zygotic genotype, as ninein knock-out females following mating with wild type males displayed normal litter size and no growth retardation among pups (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of litter sizes from different mating combinations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Examination of the uterine horns at mid-gestation, at embryonic day 9.5 post-coitum (E9.5dpc), revealed a similar number of deciduae in wild type and ninein-deleted mothers.
source: Examination of the uterine horns at mid-gestation, at embryonic day 9.5 post-coitum (E9.5dpc), revealed a similar number of deciduae in wild type and ninein-deleted mothers (8.7±0.8, n=13 vs 9.2±0.8, n=12, respectively).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of deciduae in wild type and ninein-deleted mothers.

claim: Following removal of the extraembryonic tissues, very small ninein del/del embryos were frequently found, as well as empty decidua.
source: However, following removal of the extraembryonic tissues, very small ninein del/del embryos were frequently found, as well as empty decidua (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on examination of deciduae at E9.5, with supporting image in Figure 1C.

claim: At E11.5, extremely small embryos were occasionally observed.
source: At E11.5, extremely small embryos were occasionally observed (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on observations at E11.5, with supporting image in Figure 1D.

claim: A significant reduction in the progeny occurred at mid gestation and accounted for the reduced number of pups observed at birth.
source: A significant reduction in the progeny occurred at mid gestation and accounted for the reduced number of pups observed at birth.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on observations of embryo loss at mid-gestation and reduced litter sizes at birth.

claim: Prenatal loss of embryos was largely dependent on the del/del zygotic genotype.
source: This confirmed that prenatal loss of embryos was largely dependent on the del/del zygotic genotype.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of litter sizes from different mating combinations.

claim: No external abnormalities were noticed and polydactyly was never observed upon ninein deprivation.
source: No external abnormalities were noticed and polydactyly was never observed upon ninein deprivation.
evidence: This claim is based on examination of E18.5 embryos.

claim: Visceral organs such as the liver and kidney were free of cysts in ninein-deficient mice.
source: Visceral organs such as the liver and kidney were free of cysts, in contrast to mice mutant for other proteins of centrosomes and cilia, such as Cep290 or Cc2d2a (Rachel et al., 2015; Veleri et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on examination of visceral organs and comparison to other mutant mice.

claim: Neither laterality defects nor airway defects were present in ninein del/del mice.
source: Neither laterality defects nor airway defects were present in ninein del/del mice.
evidence: This claim is based on examination of E18.5 embryos.

claim: No morphological abnormalities were noticed in sensory organs such as the eye and ear in ninein del/del mice.
source: No morphological abnormalities were noticed in sensory organs such as the eye and ear, although these were not tested functionally.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological examination of sensory organs.

claim: Examination of E18.5 embryos revealed an advanced ossification in the digits of all ninein-deficient embryos.
source: Examination of E18.5 embryos revealed an advanced ossification in the digits of all ninein-deficient embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal staining showing additional ossification centers in digits of ninein-deficient embryos.

claim: In the forelimb of control embryos at E18.5, one ossification center was detected in the metacarpal bone and in the proximal phalange of digits 2–5.
source: In the forelimb of control embryos, one ossification center was detected in the metacarpal bone and in the proximal phalange of digits 2–5 (Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In ninein-deficient embryos at E18.5, an additional mineralized area was clearly visible in the intermediate phalange of digits 2–4 of the forelimb.
source: By contrast, in mutant embryos, an additional mineralized area was clearly visible in the intermediate phalange of digits 2–4 (Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A similar advanced ossification was observed in the hindlimbs of ninein-deprived embryos at E18.5.
source: A similar advanced ossification was observed in the hindlimbs of ninein-deprived embryos (Figure 2C, right image).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The proximal phalange of digit one in the hindlimb exhibited a small ossification center in ninein del/del embryos at E18.5, which was never observed in control embryos at this stage.
source: The proximal phalange of digit one exhibited a small ossification center, which was never observed in control embryos at this stage.
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The intermediate phalanges of digits 2–4 in the hindlimb started to mineralize in ninein del/del embryos at E18.5, but not in controls.
source: The intermediate phalanges of digits 2–4 started to mineralize in ninein del/del embryos, but not in controls
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No differences in bone size were seen between control and ninein del/del embryos at E18.5.
source: However, no differences in bone size were seen in the two groups (Figure 2D, and morphometric analysis in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of dissected long bones shown in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The second cervical vertebra (axis) exhibited an additional ossification center within the cartilaginous vertebral body in ninein-deleted embryos at E18.5.
source: On the opposite, the second vertebra, the axis, exhibited an additional ossification center within the cartilaginous vertebral body in ninein-deleted embryos (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At E16.0, no ossification was visible in the upper and lower foot of control embryos.
source: In controls, no ossification was visible in the upper and lower foot.
evidence: This claim is based on alizarin red staining of E16.0 embryos shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At E16.0, two metacarpal and three metatarsal bones showed signs of mineralization in ninein del/del embryos.
source: In ninein del/del embryos, two metacarpal and three metatarsal bones showed signs of mineralization (Figure 3A, arrows).
evidence: This claim is based on alizarin red staining of E16.0 embryos shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At E16.5, control metacarpal bones 3 and 4 exhibited tiny red deposits on the internal face, but not within central metatarsal bones yet.
source: In slightly older embryos (E16.5), control metacarpal bones 3 and 4 exhibited tiny red deposits on the internal face (Figure 3B, left), but not within central metatarsal bones yet (Figure 3C, left).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining of E16.5 embryos shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: At E16.5, bone collar formation was already well visible in metacarpal and metatarsal bones of ninein-deficient embryos.
source: In ninein-deficient embryos, bone collar formation was already well visible in metacarpal and metatarsal bones (Figure 3B and C, right).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining of E16.5 embryos shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Analysis at E16.5 and E18.5dpc revealed comparable sizes of the zones of proliferating and hypertrophied chondrocytes in controls and ninein del/del embryos.
source: Analysis at E16.5 and E18.5dpc revealed comparable sizes of both zones in controls and ninein del/del embryos (Figure 3H, I)
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of chondrocyte zones shown in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: Detection of osteoblasts by alkaline phosphatase staining revealed no differences between control and ninein del/del genotypes.
source: Detection of osteoblasts, the bone-making cells, was performed by alkaline phosphatase staining and revealed no differences between both genotypes (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This claim is based on alkaline phosphatase staining shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Quantification of osteoblasts per bone length revealed similar numbers in embryos of both genotypes at E16.5 and E18.5.
source: Quantification of osteoblasts per bone length revealed similar numbers in embryos of both genotypes at E16.5 and E18.5 (Figure 3J)
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of osteoblasts shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Differences in ossification occur independently of osteoblasts in ninein-deficient embryos.
source: suggesting that differences in ossification occur independently of osteoblasts in ninein-deficient embryos.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that osteoblast numbers are similar in control and mutant embryos despite differences in ossification.

claim: At E18.5, forelimb and hindlimb digits d2 to d4 show enhanced mineralization in the ninein-deleted group.
source: Forelimb and hindlimb digits d2 to d4 show enhanced mineralization in the ninein-deleted group.
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: At 21.5dpc, the tip of the forelimb exhibited enhanced mineralization in both proximal and intermediate phalanges of digits 2–5 of ninein del/del embryos.
source: As shown in the supplement to Figure 3, the tip of the forelimb exhibited enhanced mineralization in both proximal and intermediate phalanges of digits 2–5 of ninein del/del embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 21.5dpc, in the hindlimb of ninein del/del embryos, tarsal bones displayed increased mineral deposits as well as the phalanges.
source: In the hindlimb of ninein del/del embryos, tarsal bones displayed increased mineral deposits as well as the phalanges, although to a lesser level than in forelimbs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At 21.5dpc, bones of the rib cage did not show modified mineralization in ninein del/del embryos.
source: Bones of the rib cage did not show modified mineralization.
evidence: This claim is based on examination of skeletal preparations at 21.5dpc.

claim: At 21.5dpc, the hyoid bone always displayed primary ossification centers within the greater horns in ninein-deleted pups, which was not observed yet in controls at this age.
source: By contrast, in the neck area, the hyoid bone always displayed primary ossification centers within the greater horns in ninein-deleted pups, which was not observed yet in controls at this age (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At 21.5dpc, the axis contained two small mineralized areas within the anterior cartilaginous arch in controls that were significantly enlarged in ninein-deleted embryos.
source: Among the seven cervical vertebrae, the axis contained two small mineralized areas within the anterior cartilaginous arch in controls that were significantly enlarged in ninein-deleted embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At 21.5dpc, primary ossification centers in neural arches, cervical vertebrae 3–7, were enlarged in ninein-deleted embryos.
source: Likewise, primary ossification centers in neural arches, cervical vertebrae 3–7, were enlarged in ninein-deleted embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At 21.5dpc, caudal vertebrae had an increased ossification clearly visible within the tail of ninein-deleted embryos.
source: In addition, at the most caudal end of the skeleton below the lumbar 5 vertebra, caudal vertebrae had an increased ossification clearly visible within the tail of ninein-deleted embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In ninein-deleted embryos, bone mineralization took place earlier than in controls, but this occurred without interfering with endochondral bone growth.
source: Altogether, in ninein-deleted embryos, bone mineralization took place earlier than in controls, but this occurred without interfering with endochondral bone growth.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple observations of advanced ossification without changes in bone size.

claim: At E16.5, frontal bones above the eyes were more intensely mineralized in ninein-deleted embryos than in controls.
source: Notably, frontal bones above the eyes were more intensely mineralized in ninein-deleted embryos than in controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on von Kossa staining of coronal head sections shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At E16.5, sections more posterior to the eyes revealed frontal bones with a larger trabecular structure that extends toward the interfrontal suture in ninein-deleted embryos.
source: Sections more posterior to the eyes revealed frontal bones with a larger trabecular structure that extends toward the interfrontal suture in ninein-deleted embryos (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on Alizarin red S staining shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At E16.5, dissection of skull bones coupled with area determination showed larger frontal and parietal bones in skull of mutant embryos.
source: Dissection of skull bones coupled with area determination showed larger frontal and parietal bones in skull of E16.5 mutant embryos (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of dissected skull bones shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: At E16.5, the interparietal bone was slightly longer and twice larger in ninein-deleted embryos.
source: The interparietal bone was slightly longer and twice larger (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of dissected skull bones shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At 21.5dpc, the head circumference was of the same magnitude in mutant pups as in time-mated neonate controls.
source: Although the head circumference was of the same magnitude as in time-mated neonate controls
evidence: This claim is based on examination of 21.5dpc pups.

claim: At 21.5dpc, the interparietal, parietal and frontal bones were larger in mutants, whereas the supraoccipital bone was of the same size.
source: the interparietal, parietal and frontal bones were larger in mutants, whereas the supraoccipital bone was of the same size (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining of 21.5dpc skulls shown in Figure 4E.

claim: At 21.5dpc, the interfrontal suture was significantly reduced close to the parietal bones in ninein-deleted pups.
source: Most importantly, the interfrontal suture was significantly reduced close to the parietal bones (Figure 4F)
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining shown in Figure 4F.

claim: At 21.5dpc, the interfrontal suture was obliterated between nasal bones in ninein-deleted pups.
source: and obliterated between nasal bones in ninein-deleted pups (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is based on skeletal staining shown in Figure 4G.

claim: An earlier intramembranous ossification may lead to premature closure of the skull sutures.
source: This indicates that an earlier intramembranous ossification may lead to premature closure of the skull sutures.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of increased ossification and reduced suture space.

claim: A strong signal of β-galactosidase was identified within large multinucleated cells near the growth plate of long bones and adjacent to osteoid matrix in E16.5 Nintm1a embryos.
source: We focused on developing E16.5 embryos, and following X-Gal staining, we identified a strong signal within large multinucleated cells near the growth plate of long bones and adjacent to osteoid matrix, visualized by von-Kossa-staining (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on X-Gal staining of Nintm1a embryos shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The multinucleated cells expressing β-galactosidase were confirmed to be osteoclasts by TRAP staining.
source: Histological staining of tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) was used as a marker of osteoclasts on serial sections, to confirm that the multinucleated cells were indeed osteoclasts (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on TRAP staining shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At E16.5, a significant increase of the mineralized portion of the tibia was detected in ninein del/del embryos.
source: At E16.5, a significant increase of the mineralized portion of the tibia was detected in ninein del/del embryos (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of von Kossa staining shown in Figure 5F.

claim: At E16.5, the increase in mineralized tibia was accompanied by a decrease in osteoclast cell numbers within the same area.
source: This was accompanied by a decrease in osteoclast cell numbers within the same area (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of TRAP-positive cells shown in Figure 5G.

claim: On E18.5 tibiae, increased mineralization was no longer detected although osteoclast numbers were still significantly reduced.
source: On E18.5 tibiae, increased mineralization was no longer detected although osteoclast numbers were still significantly reduced (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Scanning through the cortical and trabecular bones below the hypertrophied chondrocytes revealed no difference between control and mutants at E18.5.
source: Scanning through the cortical and trabecular bones below the hypertrophied chondrocytes revealed no difference between control and mutants (Figure 5H, I), in agreement with histology data.
evidence: This claim is based on X-ray microtomography analysis shown in Figures 5H and 5I.

claim: In a subchondral core of the tibia at E18.5, the volume occupied by mineralized bone was of the same magnitude in control and ninein-deleted embryos.
source: In a subchondral core of the tibia of 200 μm diameter and 700 μm length, the volume occupied by mineralized bone was of the same magnitude in control and ninein-deleted embryos (0.00210±0.00026 mm3 vs 0.00203±0.00006 mm3, respectively)
evidence: This claim is based on X-ray microtomography measurements.

claim: At E18.5, analysis performed in the middle of the tibiae in controls revealed that the volume of mineralized bone had reduced by 2-fold, consistent with the onset of bone marrow cavity formation.
source: Meanwhile, analysis performed in the middle of the tibiae in controls revealed that the volume of mineralized bone had reduced by 2-fold (0.00107±0.00025 mm3), consistent with the onset of bone marrow cavity formation, following blood vessel invasion in this central part of the bone (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is based on X-ray microtomography measurements shown in Figure 5J.

claim: At E18.5, in ninein-deleted embryos the volume of mineralized bone in the central area of the tibia was significantly higher as compared to controls.
source: By contrast, in ninein-deleted embryos the volume of mineralized bone in this central area was significantly higher as compared to controls (0.00193±0.00012 mm3, p<0.05; Figure 5J and K).
evidence: This claim is based on X-ray microtomography measurements shown in Figures 5J and 5K.

claim: The genesis of osteoclasts was impaired in the absence of ninein, resulting in structural changes in the developing trabecular bone of the tibia.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that the genesis of osteoclasts was impaired in the absence of ninein, resulting in structural changes in the developing trabecular bone of the tibia.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of reduced osteoclast numbers and altered bone structure.

claim: At E14.5, von-Kossa-staining revealed the absence of mineralization in both controls and ninein del/del mice.
source: On longitudinal sections of whole embryos, von-Kossa-staining revealed the absence of mineralization at this stage of development, both in controls and ninein del/del mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is based on von Kossa staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: At E14.5, TRAP enzymatic reaction indicated the presence of osteoclast progenitors in the fetal liver in all embryos.
source: On the same sections, TRAP enzymatic reaction indicated the presence of osteoclast progenitors in the fetal liver, an active site of erythro-myeloid hematopoiesis in all E14.5 embryos.
evidence: This claim is based on TRAP staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: At E14.5, two additional foci of TRAP-positive cells were observed in an area corresponding to the mandibular and maxillary bone formation.
source: Two additional foci of TRAP-positive cells were observed in an area corresponding to the mandibular and maxillary bone formation, the first bones to mineralize (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is based on TRAP staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: At E14.5, numerous TRAP-positive cells were detected close to Meckel's cartilage, in both control and ninein-deleted embryos.
source: Numerous TRAP-positive cells were detected close to Meckel's cartilage, in both control and ninein-deleted embryos (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is based on TRAP staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: At E14.5, Sirius Red staining verified that collagen deposition was effective in the mandible area, where osteoclast progenitors were detected.
source: Because the first step of bone formation involves the production of a collagenous matrix by condensed mesenchymal cells, we used Sirius Red dye to verify that collagen deposition was effective in the mandible area, where osteoclast progenitors were detected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is based on Sirius Red staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: At E14.5, the presence of bone-forming osteoblasts was confirmed using alkaline phosphatase enzymatic reaction.
source: Similarly, the presence of bone-forming osteoblasts was confirmed using alkaline phosphatase enzymatic reaction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This claim is based on alkaline phosphatase staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: At E14.5, all three staining protocols (TRAP, Sirius Red, alkaline phosphatase) yielded comparable results in control and ninein del/del siblings.
source: All three staining protocols yielded comparable results in control and ninein del/del siblings.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of staining results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E14.5, mononucleated osteoclast progenitors represented the vast majority of TRAP-positive cells.
source: Quantitative analysis of approximately 1300 cells/genotype showed that mononucleated osteoclast progenitors represented the vast majority of TRAP-positive cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of TRAP-positive cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At E14.5, mononucleated osteoclast progenitors were significantly more abundant in ninein-deleted embryos, as compared to control littermates.
source: They were significantly more abundant in ninein-deleted embryos, as compared to control littermates.
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of TRAP-positive cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At E14.5, similar percentages of binucleated osteoclasts were counted in control and ninein-deleted embryos.
source: Similar percentages of binucleated osteoclasts were counted in control and ninein-deleted E14.5 embryos.
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of TRAP-positive cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At E14.5, multinucleated osteoclasts were more than threefold reduced in ninein-deleted embryos as compared to controls.
source: However, multinucleated osteoclasts were more than threefold reduced in ninein-deleted embryos as compared to controls (Figure 6A)
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of TRAP-positive cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The initial fusion events among osteoclast progenitors were impaired at E14.5 in ninein-deleted embryos.
source: indicating that the initial fusion events among osteoclast progenitors were impaired at E14.5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of reduced multinucleated osteoclasts in ninein-deleted embryos.

claim: In neonatal bone marrow cells cultured for one hour, multinucleated osteoclasts were significantly less abundant in samples from ninein-deleted neonates.
source: Quantification of each category indicated that multinucleated osteoclasts were significantly less abundant in samples from ninein-deleted neonates, whereas single TRAP-positive cells were more numerous, in comparison to controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of TRAP-positive cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In neonatal bone marrow cells cultured for one hour, single TRAP-positive cells were more numerous in samples from ninein-deleted neonates, in comparison to controls.
source: whereas single TRAP-positive cells were more numerous, in comparison to controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of TRAP-positive cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In neonatal bone marrow cells cultured for one hour, the percentages of aggregates with unfused or fused cells were similar in both control and ninein-deleted groups.
source: The percentages of aggregates with unfused or fused cells were similar in both groups.
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of TRAP-positive cells shown in Figure 6B.

claim: From day 3 onwards in adult bone marrow cultures, control osteoclasts reached diameters of several hundred microns.
source: From day 3 onwards, control osteoclasts reached diameters of several hundred microns
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of osteoclast size in culture.

claim: In adult bone marrow cultures, the increase in cell surface correlated in a linear fashion with the number of syncytial nuclei.
source: and the increase in cell surface correlated in a linear fashion with the number of syncytial nuclei (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The largest syncytia in adult bone marrow cultures contained more than 100 nuclei.
source: The largest syncytia contained more than 100 nuclei, consistent with other reports on mouse osteoclasts in culture (Tiedemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on observations of osteoclast cultures and comparison to published reports.

claim: A comparable correlation between cell surface and number of nuclei was seen in osteoclasts from ninein-deleted bone marrow, but larger syncytia were significantly less abundant in these mutants.
source: A comparable correlation was seen in osteoclasts from ninein-deleted bone marrow, but larger syncytia were significantly less abundant in these mutants (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The fusion index of osteoclasts from ninein-knockout mice was 1.8 times lower than in cultures from control mice.
source: We found that the fusion index of osteoclasts from ninein-knockout mice was 1.8 times lower than in cultures from control mice (9% vs 16%, Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of the fusion index shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Multinucleated osteoclasts in ninein-deficient cultures covered an area that was 1.9 times smaller than in control cultures.
source: Likewise, multinucleated osteoclasts in ninein-deficient cultures covered an area that was 1.9 times smaller than in control cultures
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The total density of nuclei (combined from fused and unfused cells) was comparable for control and ninein-deficient genotypes in adult bone marrow cultures.
source: with the total density of nuclei (combined from fused and unfused cells) being comparable for the two genotypes (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: No significant differences in cell cycle profiles were detected between control and mutant cultures one day before the onset of fusion.
source: To verify whether reduced fusion in ninein-deficient cells was resulting from differences in proliferation and cell cycle progression, we established cell cycle profiles (Figure 7D), and we quantified the expression of the proliferation marker Ki-67 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) one day before the onset of fusion. No significant differences between control and mutant cultures were detected.
evidence: This claim is based on cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 7D and Ki-67 expression shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No differences in cell death were seen between control and ninein-deficient genotypes in adult bone marrow cultures.
source: To exclude the effect of cell death on osteoclastogenesis in ninein-deficient cultures, we performed co-staining with Annexin V and propidium iodide, and we controlled for the presence of cleaved poly-(ADP-ribose)-polymerase (PARP) and cleaved caspase 3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, E). Again, no differences were seen between the different genotypes.
evidence: This claim is based on Annexin V/propidium iodide staining and western blot analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: No significant differences in cell attachment of the osteoclast precursor cells were detected between control and ninein-deficient genotypes.
source: We could further exclude any significant differences in cell attachment of the osteoclast precursor cells, since numbers of adherent cells and expression profiles of beta-integrins were comparable prior to osteoclast fusion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This claim is based on cell adhesion assays and integrin expression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: Ninein-deficient osteoclast precursors exhibit specific defects in cell fusion during osteoclastogenesis.
source: In summary, our data indicate that ninein-deficient osteoclast precursors exhibit specific defects in cell fusion during osteoclastogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple observations showing reduced fusion without changes in proliferation, cell death, or attachment.

claim: Large syncytia (from 5000 to 50,000 μm2) represented less than 5% of osteoclasts of both genotypes on average.
source: On average, these large syncytia represented less than 5% of osteoclasts of both genotypes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Large syncytia were twice as abundant in control cultures on days 3 and 4, as compared to ninein-deleted samples.
source: but they were twice as abundant in control cultures on days 3 and 4, as compared to ninein-deleted samples (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: On day 5, the abundance of large syncytia lacking ninein climbed to more than 90% of control levels.
source: However, on day 5, the abundance of large syncytia lacking ninein climbed to more than 90% of control levels
evidence: This claim is based on quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fusion deficiencies are a transient phenomenon in in vitro-induced adult osteoclasts.
source: suggesting that fusion deficiencies are a transient phenomenon in in vitro-induced adult osteoclasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fusion defects are compensated by day 5 in culture.

claim: The resorption area of osteoclasts lacking ninein was approximately three times smaller than that of controls.
source: Importantly, when osteoclast function was assessed in bone resorption assays, we found that the resorption area of osteoclasts lacking ninein was approximately three times smaller than that of controls (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is based on bone resorption assays shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Mother and daughter centrioles were separated to varying degrees in the absence of ninein (mean distance 1.1 μm±0.2).
source: Staining with the centriolar marker centrin revealed that mother and daughter centrioles were separated to varying degrees in the absence of ninein (mean distance 1.1 μm±0.2, n=11 different mice)
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of centriole distances in ninein-deficient cells.

claim: In control cells, mother and daughter centrioles remained more closely associated (mean distance 0.6 μm±0.1).
source: whereas in control cells they remained more closely associated (0.6 μm±0.1, n = 7 different mice; Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of centriole distances in control cells shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Microtubule organization at the centrosome appeared less focused in cells without ninein.
source: Microtubule organization at the centrosome appeared less focused in cells without ninein, consistent with previously published results (Dammermann and Merdes, 2002; Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence shown in Figure 8B and comparison to published results.

claim: Immunofluorescence revealed a reduction of 48% of the p150 signal at centrioles in ninein del/del cells.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed a reduction of 48% of the p150 signal at centrioles in these cells (n=52; Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of p150 immunofluorescence shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The defects in precursor cells from bone marrow of adult ninein-deleted mice resembled those seen in cells from newborn mice.
source: The defects in precursor cells from bone marrow of adult ninein-deleted mice resembled those seen in cells from newborn mice
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of immunofluorescence results from adult and newborn cells.

claim: Loss of microtubule focusing was even more pronounced in precursor cells from adult bone marrow.
source: and loss of microtubule focusing was even more pronounced (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence shown in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: Upon fusion into multinucleated osteoclasts, significant differences in centrosome positioning became apparent in ninein-deleted cells.
source: Upon fusion into multinucleated osteoclasts, significant differences in centrosome positioning became apparent in ninein-deleted cells.
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence observations of multinucleated osteoclasts.

claim: The numerous centrioles in control osteoclasts were all regrouped in one or very few clusters.
source: Whereas the numerous centrioles in control osteoclasts were all regrouped in one or very few clusters
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figures 8F and 8G.

claim: The individual centrioles in osteoclasts lacking ninein were scattered or localized close to the surfaces of the syncytial nuclei.
source: the individual centrioles in osteoclasts lacking ninein were scattered or localized close to the surfaces of the syncytial nuclei (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figures 8F and 8G.

claim: Large clusters of centrioles in control osteoclasts represented focal points of microtubule organization and dynactin accumulation.
source: Large clusters of centrioles in control osteoclasts represented focal points of microtubule organization and dynactin accumulation
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figures 8F and 8G.

claim: No comparable focusing of microtubules and dynactin was visible in ninein del/del osteoclasts.
source: whereas no comparable focusing was visible in ninein del/del osteoclasts (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence observations shown in Figures 8F and 8G.

claim: 93% of control osteoclasts displayed at least one cluster, whereas only 11% of ninein del/del osteoclasts showed any clustering.
source: Quantification of centriole clustering (Figure 8H) was performed as described by Phan et al., 2004, revealing that 93% of control osteoclasts displayed at least one cluster, whereas only 11% of ninein del/del osteoclasts showed any clustering.
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of centriole clustering shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Multiple clusters were visible in medium and large control osteoclasts, but completely absent from any ninein del/del osteoclasts.
source: Moreover, multiple clusters were visible in medium and large control osteoclasts, but completely absent from any ninein del/del osteoclasts.
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of centriole clustering shown in Figure 8H.

claim: The occasional appearance of a single cluster in mutant osteoclasts of any size may be due to random proximity of centrioles, rather than active clustering.
source: The occasional appearance of a single cluster in mutant osteoclasts of any size may be due to random proximity of centrioles, rather than active clustering.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the clustering data.

claim: Osteoclast defects might be a novel element contributing to microcephaly in humans upon ninein mutation.
source: Here we propose that osteoclast defects might be a novel element contributing to microcephaly in humans upon ninein mutation, in addition to proliferative defects that impact on the overall growth of the body and the brain (Dauber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the experimental findings and comparison to human patients.

claim: The reduced percentage of multinucleated osteoclasts in the ninein-deleted embryos likely disturbs the balance between bone formation and degradation.
source: The reduced percentage of multinucleated osteoclasts in the ninein-deleted embryos likely disturbs the balance between bone formation and degradation, as mononucleated osteoclasts are thought to have a lower capacity of bone resorption.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of reduced multinucleated osteoclasts and knowledge about osteoclast function.

claim: Mononucleated osteoclasts are thought to have a lower capacity of bone resorption.
source: as mononucleated osteoclasts are thought to have a lower capacity of bone resorption.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about osteoclast function.

claim: In the microphthalmic osteopetrotic mouse, mononucleated osteoclasts result from fusion defects in very young embryos and function inefficiently in bone resorption at prenatal stages.
source: This was emphasized in an earlier report on a microphthalmic osteopetrotic mouse in which mononucleated osteoclasts result from fusion defects in very young embryos (Thesingh and Scherft, 1985). These osteoclasts function inefficiently in bone resorption at prenatal stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: One hallmark of osteopetrosis is the failure of forming a normal bone marrow cavity.
source: One hallmark of osteopetrosis is the failure of forming a normal bone marrow cavity
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about osteopetrosis.

claim: In ninein del/del embryos, delayed bone cavity formation is observed in prenatal tibiae, although osteopetrosis is not detected.
source: In our ninein del/del embryos, we observe delayed bone cavity formation in prenatal tibiae, although we do not detect osteopetrosis.
evidence: This claim is based on X-ray microtomography data showing differences in bone volume in the central tibia.

claim: The microphthalmic osteopetrotic mouse is able to produce multinucleated osteoclasts in the bone marrow ten days after birth.
source: Notably, the microphthalmic osteopetrotic mouse is able to produce multinucleated osteoclasts in the bone marrow ten days after birth, suggesting that a more mature bone marrow may compensate for earlier defects (Thesingh and Scherft, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A more mature bone marrow may compensate for earlier osteoclast defects.
source: suggesting that a more mature bone marrow may compensate for earlier defects (Thesingh and Scherft, 1985).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations in the microphthalmic osteopetrotic mouse.

claim: The fusion defects in osteoclast cultures from ninein del/del mice appear to be transient, as longer times of cell culture allowed for compensation of these defects.
source: Similarly, the fusion defects in osteoclast cultures from ninein del/del mice appear to be transient, as longer times of cell culture allowed for compensation of these defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations that fusion defects are compensated by day 5 in culture.

claim: Ninein-dependent defects may be responsible for reduced cell proliferation or cell death that may restrain growth at very early embryonic stages in ninein-KO mice.
source: Ninein-dependent defects may be responsible for reduced cell proliferation or cell death that may, at least in part, restrain growth at very early embryonic stages in ninein-KO mice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed growth defects.

claim: Abnormalities of the mitotic spindles may be at the origin of growth defects in ninein-KO mice.
source: Abnormalities of the mitotic spindles may be at the origin of these defects, since ninein has been reported to localize to the spindle poles and to prevent the formation of multipolar spindles (Logarinho et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known functions of ninein and citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of a ninein homologue in Drosophila increases the frequency of mitotic defects, even though the gene is dispensable for the viability of the fly.
source: Consistently, loss of a ninein homologue in Drosophila increases the frequency of mitotic defects, even though the gene is dispensable for the viability of the fly (Kowanda et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ninein has been shown to contribute to spindle orientation and may therefore help maintaining the pool of proliferative progenitor cells in asymmetric divisions.
source: Besides playing a role in mitotic fidelity, ninein has been shown to contribute to spindle orientation and may therefore help maintaining the pool of proliferative progenitor cells in asymmetric divisions (Lecland et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In osteoclastogenesis, the absence of ninein affects directly the fusion process of mononucleated osteoclast precursors into syncytial osteoclasts.
source: However, we demonstrate that specifically in osteoclastogenesis, the absence of ninein affects directly the fusion process of mononucleated osteoclast precursors into syncytial osteoclasts
evidence: This claim is based on multiple observations showing reduced fusion in ninein-deficient osteoclasts.

claim: Cell proliferation, attachment, and viability of osteoclast precursors in culture remain unaffected by the ninein-knockout.
source: whereas cell proliferation, attachment, and viability of precursors in culture remain unaffected by the ninein-knockout.
evidence: This claim is based on cell cycle analysis, adhesion assays, and apoptosis assays showing no differences between genotypes.

claim: An efficient fusion process is thought to require the proximity of cells, which depends on directed cell migration.
source: An efficient fusion process is thought to require the proximity of cells, which depends on directed cell migration.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about cell fusion mechanisms.

claim: Directed migration is supported by a centrosomal microtubule-organizing center that grows microtubules towards the cell's leading edge.
source: Directed migration is supported by a centrosomal microtubule-organizing center that grows microtubules towards the cell's leading edge, and to the uropod in cells undergoing amoeboid movements (Luxton and Gundersen, 2011; Kopf and Kiermaier, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of the centrosomal organizing center interferes with directional migration.
source: Loss of the centrosomal organizing center interferes with directional migration, whereas reinforcement by amplification and clustering of centrioles enhances directional migration (Wakida et al., 2010; Weier et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The fusion of precursor cells into osteoclasts is mediated by intercellular contacts.
source: The fusion of precursor cells into osteoclasts is finally mediated by intercellular contacts.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about osteoclast fusion.

claim: Fusions are thought to require local polarization of the cells and the formation of microtubule-dependent cell extensions.
source: Fusions are thought to require local polarization of the cells and the formation of microtubule-dependent cell extensions (Straube and Merdes, 2007; Dufrançais et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both directional cell migration and fusion require a strongly focused microtubule array, organized from a single centrosomal center.
source: We hypothesize that both directional cell migration and fusion require a strongly focused microtubule array, organized from a single centrosomal center.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and knowledge of cell biology.

claim: The defects in osteoclast precursors from ninein-KO mice (loss of microtubule attachment at the centrosome and splitting of the organizing center) interfere with the directionality of radial microtubule growth towards the cell periphery.
source: We believe that these defects interfere with the directionality of radial microtubule growth towards the cell periphery and thereby interfere with the directional transport of membrane vesicles, during cell migration and during the formation of plasma membrane extensions in fusing osteoclasts.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed cellular defects.

claim: Cell polarity in neurons and the initial formation of the axonal cell extension depend on centrosomal microtubules.
source: In a somewhat analogous manner, cell polarity in neurons and the initial formation of the axonal cell extension depend on centrosomal microtubules (de Anda et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Ninein-dependent microtubule anchorage and centrosome cohesion may depend, at least in part, on the interaction with the dynein/dynactin complex.
source: At the molecular level, ninein-dependent microtubule anchorage and centrosome cohesion may depend, at least in part, on the interaction with the dynein/dynactin complex.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on known interactions of ninein.

claim: An amino-terminal domain of ninein is known to bind to dynein/dynactin and to play a role in dynein activation.
source: An amino-terminal domain of ninein is known to bind to dynein/dynactin and to play a role in dynein activation (Casenghi et al., 2005; Redwine et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletions of the dynactin subunit p150 or of the dynein heavy chain cause splitting of the centrioles.
source: Depletions of the dynactin subunit p150 or of the dynein heavy chain cause splitting of the centrioles (Kodani et al., 2013; Malik et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletions of the dynein regulator proteins Lis1 and Nde1 interfere with the motility and fusion of osteoclast precursors.
source: Moreover, depletions of the dynein regulator proteins Lis1 and Nde1 interfere with the motility and fusion of osteoclast precursors, and Lis1-depletion also leads to altered microtubule organization in osteoclasts (Ye et al., 2011; Das et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A dynein/dynactin-dependent mechanism may contribute to the clustering of the numerous centrioles observed in multinucleated osteoclasts.
source: A dynein/dynactin-dependent mechanism may equally contribute to the clustering of the numerous centrioles observed in multinucleated osteoclasts (Phan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on known functions of dynein/dynactin and citation to previous work.

claim: Centriole clusters provide large focal points for microtubule organization and may thereby support cell extensions, for fusion with additional precursors into even larger syncytia.
source: In addition to perinuclear microtubule-organizing centers, these centriole clusters provide large focal points for microtubule organization and may thereby support cell extensions, for fusion with additional precursors into even larger syncytia (Mulari et al., 2003; Phan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: Clustered centrioles appear to be necessary for osteoclast polarity and secretory processes.
source: Furthermore, clustered centrioles appear to be necessary for osteoclast polarity and secretory processes (Lee et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The quantity of dynactin at the centrosome is largely reduced in the absence of ninein.
source: As we demonstrate here, the quantity of dynactin at the centrosome is largely reduced in the absence of ninein
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of p150 immunofluorescence.

claim: Clustering of centrioles fails to take place in the absence of ninein.
source: and clustering of centrioles fails to take place.
evidence: This claim is based on quantification of centriole clustering in osteoclasts.

claim: A self-centering force on the centrioles, dependent on ninein-bound dynein/dynactin may be required for centriole clustering.
source: As in mononucleated precursor cells, a self-centering force on the centrioles, dependent on ninein-bound dynein/dynactin may be required for this clustering process.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed defects and known functions of ninein and dynein/dynactin.

claim: Ninein may play a direct role as a linker component between centrioles.
source: In addition, ninein may play a direct role as a linker component between centrioles, as suggested from recent experiments in various human cell lines (Theile et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on citation to a recent study.

claim: Homozygous missense mutations in the ninein gene of patients with spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia were shown to alter the carboxy-terminal domain of ninein (N2082D), in an area that mediates the interaction with the centriolar linker protein cNap1.
source: Interestingly, homozygous missense mutations in the ninein gene of patients with spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia were shown to alter the carboxy-terminal domain of ninein (N2082D), in an area that mediates the interaction with the centriolar linker protein cNap1 (Grosch et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: cNap1 is directly involved in maintaining centrosome cohesion.
source: Since cNap1 is directly involved in maintaining centrosome cohesion (Mayor et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Centriole-splitting may contribute to ossification defects.
source: it is conceivable that centriole-splitting contributes to ossification defects.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed centriole splitting and ossification defects.

claim: A truncation mutation in cNap1 in cows is at the origin of centriole splitting and cell migration defects, as well as Seckel-like syndromes.
source: Furthermore, a truncation mutation in cNap1 in cows is at the origin of centriole splitting and cell migration defects, as well as Seckel-like syndromes (Floriot et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Clustering of centrioles may contribute to the functionality of placental cells and thereby insure early embryonic growth.
source: Clustering of centrioles may also contribute to the functionality of placental cells and thereby insure early embryonic growth, since specialized cells of the embryonic trophoectoderm, trophoblast giant cells, are polyploid and display centrosome amplification (Klisch et al., 2017; Buss et al., 2022), with clustered centrioles identified in binucleate bovine trophoblast cells (Klisch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Early embryonic growth defects in ninein-deficient mouse embryos may be explained in part by impaired centriole clustering, in addition to potential abnormalities in proliferation and cell death.
source: Thus, early embryonic growth defects in our ninein-deficient mouse embryos may be explained in part by impaired centriole clustering, in addition to potential abnormalities in proliferation and cell death.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the observed defects and known functions of centriole clustering.

claim: Ninein may regulate the number of microtubules attached at the centrosome.
source: Besides contributing to centrosome cohesion, ninein may regulate the number of microtubules attached at the centrosome (Dammermann and Merdes, 2002)
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on citation to a previous study.

claim: Ninein may anchor microtubules via dynein/dynactin or via the ninein-interactor Cep170 that has direct microtubule-binding affinity.
source: either by holding onto microtubule minus-ends via dynein/dynactin, or via the ninein-interactor Cep170 that has direct microtubule-binding affinity (Quintyne et al., 1999; Welburn and Cheeseman, 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Ninein may anchor microtubules to the subdistal appendages, as well as to the proximal regions of the centriolar surface.
source: Ninein may thus anchor microtubules to the subdistal appendages, as well as to the proximal regions of the centriolar surface (Mogensen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on citation to a previous study.

claim: Ninein may not affect the nucleation of centrosomal microtubules, as there is no significant reduction of gamma-tubulin at the centrosomes of ninein-depleted cells.
source: However, in contrast to earlier proposals (Delgehyr et al., 2005), ninein may not affect the nucleation of centrosomal microtubules, as we see no significant reduction of gamma-tubulin at the centrosomes of ninein-depleted cells.
evidence: This claim is based on immunofluorescence observations showing no reduction in gamma-tubulin at centrosomes.

claim: Independent of its centrosomal function, ninein may play a role in the recruitment of F-actin fibers to cortical sites by interacting with dynein/dynactin.
source: Independent of its centrosomal function, ninein may play a role in the recruitment of F-actin fibers to cortical sites by interacting with dynein/dynactin, as highlighted in a recent study on macrophages (Omer et al., 2024)
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on citation to a recent study.

claim: Ninein-knockout may cause subtle alterations in the actin cytoskeleton in osteoclast precursors.
source: raising the question whether ninein-knockout may cause subtle alterations in the actin cytoskeleton in osteoclast precursors.
evidence: This is a speculative question raised by the authors based on recent findings.

claim: The ninein-dependent defects at the cellular level are subtle, since osteoclast fusion still takes place, albeit less efficiently.
source: Altogether, the ninein-dependent defects at the cellular level are subtle, since osteoclast fusion still takes place, albeit less efficiently.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the observation that fusion is reduced but not completely abolished.

claim: Point mutations in ninein have been linked to Seckel syndrome, manifested by dwarfism and microcephaly, in addition to skeletal dysplasia in human patients.
source: In human patients, point mutations in ninein have been linked to Seckel syndrome, manifested by dwarfism and microcephaly, in addition to skeletal dysplasia (Dauber et al., 2012; Grosch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is tempting to speculate whether ossification defects due to a reduced pool of multinucleated osteoclasts are at the origin of skeletal abnormalities in patients with ninein mutations.
source: While the mechanisms leading to dysplasias in these patients remain unknown, it is tempting to speculate whether ossification defects due to a reduced pool of multinucleated osteoclasts are at the origin of these abnormalities.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings and comparison to human patients.
